prompt:
今回のテーマについて、Webで調査し、Verified Fact Ledgerの下書きを作成してください。

【今回のテーマ】
Current topic: is personalized news good for us? Many news apps, social platforms, and search engines now use algorithms to personalize the news people see, based on their past clicks, interests, and behavior. Aim: cover this topic in a way that makes both sides strongly true at once, not a simple good-vs-bad framing. On one side, personalization makes news consumption more convenient and relevant: it saves people time, surfaces stories that match their actual interests, and helps people cut through information overload. On the other side, personalization raises real concerns: filter bubbles (seeing mostly information that confirms existing views), worldview narrowing (a shrinking, self-reinforcing range of perspectives and topics over time), and editorial control shifting from human editors to opaque ranking algorithms with commercial incentives. Use only facts confirmed by web search (no invented details, no facts supplied from the assistant's own prior knowledge).

【役割】
あなたはResearcherです。以下を行いません:
- 記事本文を書く
- Narrativeを作る
- 比喩を考える
- 阪神マスターのstyleを模倣する
あなたが行うのは、Factだけを収集・整理することです。

【Source優先順位】
1. 政府・規制当局等の一次資料
2. 公式調査・報告書
3. 信頼できる二次資料
一次Sourceで確認できるFactを、二次Sourceだけで確定しないでください。

【特に注意して構造化すべき観点(今回のテーマに当てはまる場合のみ)】

1. 対象範囲: 年齢・人数・期間・地域等、Factが適用される範囲(scope)を数値の母集団と混同せずに特定する
2. 制度・仕様の適用条件: default設定なのか常時適用なのか、変更・例外が認められるか等、時間的・条件的scopeを明確にする。一次資料内で表現が揺れている場合は、より明確な一次Sourceを追加で検索する。それでも確定できない場合は、断定せずambiguityフィールドへその旨を明記する
3. 数値の内訳: ある数字が全体を指すのか、特定のサブグループ・条件を指すのかを明確にする。一次資料で直接確認できる場合のみnumeric_valueとして確定し、確認できない場合は推測で数字を作らず、numeric_valueをnullにしてambiguityへその旨を記録する
4. 観察・相関・因果の区別: 変化・効果・傾向等について、観察・報告なのか、相関なのか、Source自身が因果関係を主張しているのかを、causal_strengthで区別する。Sourceより強い因果表現(caused/produced/proved等)を後工程のwriterが使わないよう、causal_strengthとnotes_for_writerで明示する

【出力形式】
各Factについて、fact_id・claim・subject・date_or_period・scope・conditions・numeric_value・
numeric_scope・causal_strength・source_title・source_url・source_type・support_level・
ambiguity・notes_for_writerを埋めてください(該当しない項目はnullで構いません)。
数字・期間・対象範囲があるFactについては、該当項目を必ず明示してください。

facts.claim: Facebook describes its News Feed as a ranked system that uses signals such as who a person follows, likes, or recently engages with, and predicts the likelihood that the person will be interested in or engage with each post.
facts.subject: Facebook Feed ranking
facts.scope: Facebook News Feed; Meta's description of its ranking system
facts.conditions: The ranking system operates on candidate posts available to each user and orders them by predicted relevance or engagement.
facts.numeric_value: More than 1,000 candidate posts per person per day and thousands of signals, according to Meta's example description
facts.numeric_scope: Meta's stated system-scale description, not an independently audited universal constant
facts.source_title: How Does News Feed Predict What You Want to See? ([about.fb.com](https://about.fb.com/news/2021/01/how-does-news-feed-predict-what-you-want-to-see/?utm_source=openai))
facts.ambiguity: The source is a company description and does not disclose the complete ranking model or all current signals.
facts.notes_for_writer: Use this as evidence that ranking, not only user subscription, determines prominence. Avoid claiming that engagement is the sole objective.

facts.claim: A Reuters Institute survey across 27 markets found that close to half of respondents were comfortable with automated selection of news based on previous preferences, although comfort with personalization was lower for news than for weather, music, and online television.
facts.subject: Public comfort with personalized news selection
facts.conditions: The measure concerns comfort with websites or apps automatically selecting content based on previous preferences.
facts.numeric_value: 27 markets; close to half of respondents
facts.numeric_scope: Market count and approximate share of survey respondents
facts.source_title: How audiences think about news personalisation in the AI era ([reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2025/how-audiences-think-about-news-personalisation-ai-era))
facts.ambiguity: The page text gives an approximate share rather than the exact percentage; the chart's underlying numerical values are not reproduced in the text.
facts.notes_for_writer: Treat this as reported comfort, not proof that personalization improves news outcomes.

facts.claim: In open-ended responses analyzed by the Reuters Institute, people who were comfortable with personalized news commonly described it as more relevant to their lives and more efficient because it helped them avoid uninteresting topics or time spent viewing everything.
facts.subject: Perceived convenience and relevance
facts.scope: Open-ended comments from a subset of countries within the Reuters Institute study
facts.conditions: These are respondents' reported perceptions, not experimentally measured time savings or comprehension gains.
facts.source_title: How audiences think about news personalisation in the AI era ([reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2025/how-audiences-think-about-news-personalisation-ai-era))
facts.ambiguity: The exact number of open-ended respondents and countries in this subset is not stated on the cited page.
facts.notes_for_writer: Use 'respondents described' or 'perceived' rather than claiming measured time savings.

facts.claim: In the United States portion of the Reuters Institute's 2016 survey, 37% said automatically selecting stories based on their own past consumption was a good way to get news, compared with 22% for selection by editors and journalists and 17% for selection based on friends' consumption.
facts.subject: Preference for selection method
facts.scope: United States respondents; the report also covered 26 countries overall
facts.conditions: The question asked respondents to rate each selection method as a good way to get news.
facts.numeric_scope: United States respondents: past-consumption personalization; editors/journalists; friends' consumption, respectively
facts.source_title: People Want Personalised Recommendations (Even as They Worry about the Consequences) ([reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/archive/essays/2016/people-want-personalised-recommendations/))
facts.notes_for_writer: This is a stated preference measure from 2016, not a measure of actual usage or news quality.

facts.claim: In the United States portion of the Reuters Institute's 2016 survey, 60% said they worried personalized news could cause them to miss important information, 59% worried about missing challenging viewpoints, and 49% worried about greater privacy risk.
facts.subject: Reported concerns about personalization
facts.scope: United States respondents; the report covered 26 countries overall
facts.conditions: The question asked whether respondents were concerned about specific possible consequences of more personalized news.
facts.numeric_scope: United States respondents: missing important information; missing challenging viewpoints; privacy risk, respectively
facts.source_title: People Want Personalised Recommendations (Even as They Worry about the Consequences) ([reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/archive/essays/2016/people-want-personalised-recommendations/))
facts.notes_for_writer: The same survey records both support for personalized selection and concern about its consequences.

facts.claim: A study of browsing histories from 50,000 U.S.-located regular online-news users found that use of social networks and search engines was associated with greater mean ideological distance between individuals, while also being associated with greater exposure to material from each individual's less-preferred political side.
facts.subject: Ideological diversity and segregation in online news use
facts.scope: 50,000 U.S.-located users who regularly read online news
facts.conditions: The findings are observational associations across consumption channels; they do not establish that personalization alone caused the differences.
facts.source_title: Filter Bubbles, Echo Chambers, and Online News Consumption ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2363701?utm_source=openai))
facts.ambiguity: The study examines channels including social networks and web search; it does not isolate every individual platform's personalization system.
facts.notes_for_writer: This fact supports both greater ideological separation across users and some increased exposure to opposing material; do not reduce it to a one-direction filter-bubble finding.

facts.claim: The same 2016 browsing-history study reported that most online-news consumption consisted of users directly visiting the homepages of their favorite, typically mainstream, news outlets, which the authors said tempered both the positive and negative consequences of social networks and search engines; the reported effects were relatively modest.
facts.subject: Overall composition of online news consumption
facts.conditions: The claim concerns the study sample and its measured browsing behavior.
facts.source_title: Filter Bubbles, Echo Chambers, and Online News Consumption ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2363701?utm_source=openai))
facts.notes_for_writer: Avoid implying that social feeds or search engines account for all online news exposure.

facts.claim: A study of 10.1 million U.S. Facebook users found that Facebook's algorithmically ranked News Feed reduced exposure to ideologically cross-cutting news relative to the content shared by users' friends, but users' own choices about what to click reduced such exposure more than algorithmic ranking did.
facts.subject: Algorithmic ranking versus user choice
facts.scope: 10.1 million U.S. Facebook users who interacted with socially shared news
facts.conditions: The study measured exposure and clicks in an observational dataset; it did not randomly assign users to different ranking systems.
facts.source_title: Exposure to ideologically diverse news and opinion on Facebook ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaa1160?utm_source=openai))
facts.ambiguity: The study's results concern the Facebook environment and the period observed; they do not establish that user choice always dominates algorithmic effects on every platform.
facts.notes_for_writer: This is evidence against a purely algorithm-driven explanation, not evidence that algorithmic ranking has no effect.

facts.claim: During the 2020 U.S. presidential election, content from politically like-minded sources constituted a majority of what active adult Facebook users saw, although political information and news made up only a small fraction of total exposures.
facts.subject: Prevalence of like-minded exposure
facts.scope: Entire population of active adult Facebook users in the United States, according to the study's platform-level analysis
facts.conditions: The claim concerns source alignment across all types of Facebook content, not only news articles.
facts.source_title: Like-minded sources on Facebook are prevalent but not polarizing ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06297-w?utm_source=openai))
facts.ambiguity: The cited abstract does not give the exact majority percentage for the platform-level population analysis.
facts.notes_for_writer: Distinguish 'like-minded sources' across Facebook content from political news specifically.

facts.claim: In a field experiment involving 23,377 U.S.-based adult Facebook users, reducing exposure to content from like-minded sources from an average of 53.7% in the control group to 36.2% in the treatment group increased exposure to cross-cutting sources and reduced exposure to uncivil content, but produced no measurable effect on preregistered political attitudes such as affective polarization, ideological extremity, candidate evaluations, and belief in false claims.
facts.subject: Experimental effect of reducing like-minded exposure
facts.scope: 23,377 consenting U.S.-based adult Facebook users during the 2020 presidential election
facts.conditions: Treatment downranked content of any type from friends, groups, and Pages predicted to share the participant's political leaning.
facts.numeric_value: 23,377 users; 53.7% control exposure; 36.2% treatment exposure; approximately one-third reduction
facts.numeric_scope: Experiment sample and average share of views from like-minded sources during the treatment period
facts.source_title: Like-minded sources on Facebook are prevalent but not polarizing ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06297-w?utm_source=openai))
facts.ambiguity: The experiment lasted about three months and studied existing Facebook users; it does not estimate effects of first exposure or cumulative exposure over many years.
facts.notes_for_writer: Use the null result only for the measured period and outcomes; do not write that like-minded exposure can never affect attitudes.

facts.claim: In a two-wave study during the 2018 and 2020 U.S. elections, participants engaged with more identity-congruent and unreliable news sources through Google Search than they were exposed to in their search results; the authors concluded that user choices, rather than algorithmic curation, were the primary driver of these differences in the study.
facts.subject: Exposure versus engagement on Google Search
facts.scope: Participants in a two-wave study combining surveys with ecologically measured Google Search exposure and engagement
facts.conditions: The study compared URLs shown in search results with URLs selected by users; it did not treat all exposure as consumption.
facts.source_title: Users choose to engage with more partisan news than they are exposed to on Google Search ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06078-5?utm_source=openai))
facts.ambiguity: The findings concern Google Search during two U.S. election periods and should not be generalized automatically to social feeds or non-election periods.
facts.notes_for_writer: This fact qualifies filter-bubble claims by separating what a system shows from what users choose to open.

facts.claim: In a 2020-election experiment, assigning Facebook and Instagram users to reverse-chronological feeds instead of default algorithmic feeds substantially reduced time spent and activity on the platforms, increased exposure to political and untrustworthy content on both platforms, and did not significantly change issue polarization, affective polarization, political knowledge, or other key attitudes during the three-month study period.
facts.subject: Effects of replacing algorithmic feeds with chronological feeds
facts.scope: Consenting Facebook and Instagram users assigned to reverse-chronological feeds
facts.conditions: The treatment replaced the default algorithmic ordering with reverse chronology; outcomes were measured during the study period.
facts.source_title: How do social media feed algorithms affect attitudes and behavior in an election campaign? ([networkscienceinstitute.org](https://www.networkscienceinstitute.org/publications/how-do-social-media-feed-algorithms-affect-attitudes-and-behavior-in-an-election-campaign))
facts.ambiguity: The source page does not state the full sample size; the null effects are limited to the measured outcomes and study period.
facts.notes_for_writer: The experiment shows that large changes in exposure and engagement can coexist with no detectable short-run change in measured political attitudes.

facts.claim: An independent 2023 field experiment on X assigned active U.S. users to algorithmic or chronological feeds for an average of about seven weeks; switching from chronological to algorithmic increased engagement and shifted policy and current-political-news attitudes in a more conservative direction, while producing no significant change in affective polarization or self-reported partisanship.
facts.subject: Political effects of X's algorithmic feed
facts.date_or_period: July to September 2023 experiment; published February 18, 2026
facts.scope: 4,965 active U.S. X users who completed the main pre- and post-treatment surveys
facts.conditions: Participants were randomly assigned to X's algorithmic For You feed or chronological Following feed; the experiment studied X's 2023 feed system.
facts.numeric_value: 4,965 participants; approximately 7 weeks; +0.12 standard deviations on the aggregated policy/current-political-news index for the chronological-to-algorithmic switch
facts.numeric_scope: Main completed sample, average treatment duration, and reported composite outcome
facts.source_title: The political effects of X's feed algorithm ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10098-2?utm_source=openai))
facts.ambiguity: The result is platform-, country-, period-, and algorithm-specific; the paper cautions that it may not generalize to algorithms that amplify both ideological sides similarly.
facts.notes_for_writer: This is evidence that effects can differ by platform and direction of switching. Do not present it as a universal effect of all personalization.

facts.claim: A Congressional Research Service report states that social-media operators use algorithms based on user behavior and revealed preferences, including clicks, likes, shares, and search history, and can tune these systems toward business goals such as maximizing engagement and advertising revenue.
facts.subject: Commercial and behavioral incentives in algorithmic ranking
facts.date_or_period: Congressional Research Service report accessed September 14, 2026
facts.scope: Social-media content dissemination systems generally; not a finding about one named platform's current algorithm
facts.conditions: The report describes common platform practices and incentives, not a universal rule for every service.
facts.source_title: Social Media: Content Dissemination and Moderation Practices ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R46662/R46662.7.pdf?utm_source=openai))
facts.ambiguity: The report summarizes documented industry practices; it does not establish that every ranking decision is driven primarily by commercial incentives.
facts.notes_for_writer: Use 'can be tuned toward' or 'are described as pursuing' rather than claiming that commercial incentives always override editorial or public-interest goals.

facts.claim: The Federal Trade Commission reported that companies in its study used algorithms, data analytics, or AI to personalize content based on users' information and activities, predict what content would interest or engage a particular user, and rank the order in which content was presented; the report also said that many companies' business models incentivized mass collection of user data for targeted advertising and revenue generation.
facts.subject: Data collection, personalization, and monetization
facts.scope: Nine social-media and video-streaming companies examined through FTC Section 6(b) orders
facts.conditions: The report concerns the companies and practices covered by the FTC inquiry; it is not a universal audit of all news apps.
facts.numeric_scope: Companies covered by the FTC Section 6(b) inquiry
facts.source_title: A Look Behind the Screens: Examining the Data Practices of Social Media and Video Streaming Services ([ftc.gov](https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/Social-Media-6b-Report-9-11-2024.pdf?_bhlid=879420f696fccd4805ede733cb28b8ffc42de707&utm_source=openai))
facts.ambiguity: The report describes information supplied by the companies and FTC staff findings; it does not independently reveal each platform's complete ranking code.
facts.notes_for_writer: This supports concern about opaque incentives and data use, but not a claim that personalized news is necessarily manipulated.

facts.claim: Under Article 27 of the EU Digital Services Act, online platforms using recommender systems must explain the main parameters used and the options users have to modify or influence them; under Article 38, very large online platforms and very large online search engines must provide at least one recommender-system option that is not based on profiling.
facts.subject: Legal transparency and non-profiling alternatives
facts.date_or_period: Digital Services Act Regulation (EU) 2022/2065; applicable legal framework accessed September 14, 2026
facts.scope: Online platforms using recommender systems under Article 27; very large online platforms and very large online search engines under Article 38
facts.conditions: Article 38's non-profiling alternative applies to designated very large online platforms and very large online search engines, not every app or website.
facts.ambiguity: The regulation creates transparency and choice obligations; it does not itself establish that the resulting systems are unbiased or that users will select non-profiled options.
facts.notes_for_writer: Use as evidence that policymakers treat recommender-system parameters and profiling as governance issues, not as proof that transparency solves the underlying risks.

facts.claim: The Nature study on reducing like-minded Facebook exposure explicitly states that its design could not capture effects of prior Facebook use or cumulative exposure over years, and that longer experiments or studies among new users would be needed to assess those possibilities.
facts.subject: Limits of short-run experimental evidence
facts.scope: 23,377 U.S. adult Facebook users in the intervention study
facts.conditions: The limitation applies to interpreting the study's null effects on political attitudes.
facts.numeric_value: Three-month intervention; cumulative exposure over years not measured
facts.numeric_scope: Study duration and unmeasured longer-term period
facts.source_title: Like-minded sources on Facebook are prevalent but not polarizing ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06297-w?utm_source=openai))
facts.notes_for_writer: Do not convert a short-run null result into a claim that worldview narrowing over long periods has been ruled out.
